Student Voice

Reporting is not tattling

In Ms. Felker’s first grade group, students worked through one of the trickiest parts of the bullying arc — the difference between tattling and reporting. Tattling tries to get someone in trouble; reporting helps keep someone safe. Watch a first grade class put that difference in their own words.

Counselor’s Corner

From the counselors

🌟 Your Weekly Coping Skill: The 10-Second Pause

We all have moments when someone says something that gets on our nerves, a class feels overwhelming, or we want to react right away.

This week, try the 10-Second Pause!

Before you respond when you’re frustrated: STOP → BREATHE → THINK → CHOOSE

Take 10 seconds to ask yourself: What am I feeling? What could happen if I react right now? What response will help me, not make things worse?

This week’s challenge: Try using the 10-second pause at least once this week when you’re annoyed, frustrated, or upset. You don’t have to ignore your feelings — you’re simply giving yourself a moment to decide what to do with them.

Counselor tip: Having a feeling isn’t the problem. What we choose to do with that feeling is where our power comes in. Be patient with yourself, take the pause, and give yourself a chance to choose your response. 💙
— The Counseling Team

What’s happening with students

Counselors are building a monthly classroom-lesson sequence for grades 5–8. September begins with Meet Your Counselor — what counselors can help with, when students should reach out, and how to access support. The year then moves through organization, study skills, test anxiety, communication, goal setting, healthy relationships, personal boundaries/sexual harassment, and digital citizenship/end-of-year reflection.

DBRC

Daily Behavior Report Cards

DBRCs are into week twoWeek 2

Two refinements are now built into the rubric: observable descriptors for the mid-scale ratings, so a rating means the same thing in every room, and the dismissal rating consolidated into the final instructional block. Rate each block as it happens in Emergent Tree; students carry the printed rubric so they can track themselves in real time. DBRC is the Tier 2 layer of the MTSS flow — DBRC → DBRC + skills → ASPIRE + skills — entered through the MTSS Behavior Request with Tier 1 supports documented.

This Monday, Aug. 24, we run an end-of-day DBRC data review to strengthen daily documentation and follow-through.

Everything you need

Select your students and complete daily documentation through the Emergent Tree site. Students carry a printed rubric so they can track how they are doing in real time, not just hear about it at the end of the day.

80–100% Club
Did you know?

Across a school day, students tend to hear far more correction than encouragement. Effective classrooms aim for the opposite balance — a target of at least five positive interactions for every one correction, the 5-to-1 ratio.

Make the praise specific. “Thank you for lining up quietly with your hands to yourself” reteaches the expectation; “good job” does not. Naming the behavior you want is what makes it more likely to happen again.

Students should know two things can be true at once: I care about you. And this behavior still needs to change.
Brad Weinstein · @WeinsteinEdu
Your Resources

Requesting behavior support

What each one is, and how it reaches you.

The MTSS Behavior Request

The MTSS Behavior Request is how you request behavior support for a student. It brings the student to our team, documents what you have already tried in your room, and starts the process of matching the right support to the need. DBRCs are requested here.

Every teacher received a 1:1 walkthrough of the MTSS Behavior Request this week. If the process is still fuzzy, grab a restorative team member and we will run it together.
